title: Out-of-control SUV comes to rest in tree on north Durango property
body: It was an unusual sight, this Toyota SUV propped on top of another vehicle leaning against a house and a tree. The unusual scene was the result of the SUV leaving the right side of north Main Avenue, barreling down a slight embankment, narrowly avoiding trees, hitting a vehicle parked in a driveway and being launched about 10 feet into the air. The Toyota came to rest on top of the parked vehicle. It damaged a garage roof and became tangled with a juniper tree. The crash occurred about 10:20 a.m. Thursday in the 3700 block of north Main Avenue, just north of the Animas View Drive intersection, according to Durango Police Department. The vehicle was traveling north – likely at a high rate of speed – when it left the road and darted toward the house. The crash occurred right where the speed limit switches from 35 mph to 55 mph. Jim Ruetschle, homeowner, was sitting inside his living room watching TV when he heard the crash. “It was like an airplane hit the house – and that’s an accurate quote,” he said. Ruetschle said he walked outside and saw a cloud of dust. He then saw the Toyota on top of his 2023 Ford Explorer and heard the screams of a man clearly in pain. “There was a guy who was just screaming up there in the car,” Ruetschle said. “He stuck his head out. ... He was just in a lot of pain, obviously.” Ruetschle, who recently underwent a hip replacement, was in no condition to climb onto the roof to assist the driver. He notified law enforcement, and medics eventually moved the man into the backseat of the SUV and freed him through a rear passenger door. The man, who had not been identified as of 2 p.m., was able to stand but was clearly in pain. He was loaded onto a stretcher and wheeled into an ambulance. Police said the cause of the crash was under investigation. It was unknown why the driver left the road or how fast he may have been traveling. “Based on the distance that the vehicle traveled after leaving the highway, I would anticipate that understanding the speed of the vehicle is going to be a big component of trying to figure out what happened – if that makes sense,” said Cmdr. Jacob Dunlop, with the Durango Police Department. The Colorado State Patrol was called to help investigate the mechanics of the crash. The vehicle is registered to a local resident, DPD said. Ruetschle, who has lived at the house for 28 years, said this is the fourth or fifth time a driver has flown off the embankment above his house and come crashing down into his property. It is the third time in the past year, said his wife, Ann, who was working at the Durango Public Library at the time of the crash. He said drivers tend to step on the gas and drive “like a bat out of hell” as they prepare to leave city limits – traveling north on U.S. Highway 550, where the speed limit switches from 35 mph to 55 mph. He hopes this latest crash will convince the city of Durango or the Colorado Department of Transportation to lower the speed limit and install a guardrail above his property. “We don't normally have vehicles that crash into houses. They usually stay on the roadway,” said DPD spokeswoman Amanda Garrison. “But it's not unheard of, especially in situations where we have roads above houses it tends to be a little more likely.” shane@durangoherald.com  Choose from several print and digital subscription packages Sign up for our daily email newsletter or to receive breaking news delivered to your inbox: © 2026 Tri-City Record |         Ballantine Communications, Inc. title: Pueblo leaders, federal lawmakers ramp up calls to keep Chaco drilling buffer
body: Representatives from 20 pueblos joined New Mexico’s congressional delegates at the U.S. Capitol on Wednesday to repeat a simple message: “Chaco Canyon is not for sale.” State and federal Democratic lawmakers and tribal leaders – whose ancestors built a major city there more than a millennium ago – have long made clear their opposition to the Trump administration’s plans to rescind a 10-mile buffer zone barring drilling and mineral extraction around Chaco Culture National Historical Park in northwestern New Mexico. Chaco Canyon “is a vibrant place of prayer, pilgrimage and core to the identity of many Southwest tribes, whose connection to this land stretches back thousands of years,” U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez said at Wednesday’s news conference in Washington, D.C. “In other words, there is no replacing it. The administration’s decision to revoke protections for the greater Chaco landscape are an absolute gut punch to New Mexico and to our pueblos, and to give just the public 14 days to respond is an insult.” Aligning with the Trump administration’s focus on removing restrictions on mining and oil and gas extraction, the Bureau of Land Management plans to revoke a 2023 order closing about 336,404 acres near Chaco Canyon to drilling and mining for 20 years. The order was issued by then-Interior Secretary Deb Haaland, the New Mexico Democratic gubernatorial nominee. Supporters of the buffer zone have been ramping up their public outreach efforts as a two-week public comment period on the environmental assessment for the plan to allow mining and drilling, which they have decried as too short, approaches its end July 29. “The question before us is simple: What kind of legacy will we leave?” Cochiti Pueblo Gov. Phillip Quintana said. “Will we choose short-term extraction, or will we choose to protect one of the most important Indigenous cultural landscapes in North America, a place whose meaning reaches far beyond any single administration?” New Mexico’s five Democratic senators and members of Congress on Wednesday wrote to U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, asking him to extend the comment period to at least 90 days. The letter also calls on Burgum to visit Chaco “before taking any action that would put this irreplaceable landscape at risk,” something he agreed to do in an appearance before the House Natural Resource Committee in June 2025. “He lied,” U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, whose district includes Chaco Canyon, said Wednesday. “But we will hold him to his comment. We will hold the Department of Interior to the rules and the laws and the regulations and we will not let them silence us.” “We asked for a meeting, but we never got it,” said Joey Sanchez, chair of the All Pueblo Council of Governors. “I don’t know if you’re here in town, but you know we’re here. We’re ready to be with you. We ask you to come and visit.” Burgum did not respond to requests for comment. Although the decision on whether to revoke the buffer zone is being made at the federal level, state Rep. Derrick Lente, D-Sandia Pueblo, doesn’t want the state to sit idly by. “I am calling on the governor to make New Mexico’s opposition unmistakable and to direct the resources of the state toward defending this landscape,” Lente said in a Tuesday statement. Lente said the state Department of Cultural Affairs and the State Historic Preservation Officer should “use their full authority in the federal review process, including their formal role under the National Historic Preservation Act, to insist that the cultural harm of this proposal be honestly studied and honestly weighed.” A spokesperson for Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham said she has been “pushing back on this terribly shortsighted and reckless proposal for months, including submitting official administration correspondence in April and coordinating with New Mexico’s congressional delegation to bolster our state’s official opposition.” Although leaders of New Mexico pueblos have been united in publicly opposing drilling and mining around Chaco, leaders of the Navajo Nation, whose lands surround Chaco Canyon, have often disagreed. Navajo President Buu Nygren, who opposes the buffer zone, will not be returning to office next year, having come in third in Tuesday’s primary election. However, the two candidates to succeed him have expressed views on the topic that are fundamentally the same as his. Justin Jones has said allottees should be allowed to develop oil and gas extraction “because they have surface and subsurface possessory rights,” the Navajo Times reported in 2022. And Crystalyne Curley, the Navajo Nation Council speaker, strongly disagreed with Haaland’s 2023 decision to impose the 10-mile buffer. However, their perspective isn’t the only one in the area. Mario Atencio, a Navajo activist and critic of the oil and gas industry’s impact on his home whose family has allotments within the buffer zone, said Wednesday revoking protections would give the government “free rein to pollute the land.” “It’s challenging and detrimental to the public health of local people,” he said. Searchlight New Mexico is a nonprofit, nonpartisan media organization that seeks to empower New Mexicans to demand honest and effective public policy. title: New Mexico insurers refused to renew policies for record number of homes in 2025, official says
body: National insurers opted not to renew more than 6,200 homeowners’ insurance policies in New Mexico in 2025, marking the highest-ever number of non-renewals in the state amid increasing industry fears of wildfires, floods and other disasters. The number of non-renewals each year has nearly tripled since 2021, when insurers opted not to renew policies for roughly 2,200 homeowners, according to figures that state Insurance Superintendent Alice Kane presented Tuesday to lawmakers on the Legislative Finance Committee. The sharp increase has prompted the New Mexico Office of the Superintendent of Insurance, which Kane oversees, to step up its data collection from the state’s top 10 insurers to better identify why homeowners are losing their policies. So far, homeowners in Rio Arriba, Taos, Sandoval and Santa Fe counties appear to be most at risk, Kane said. “The majority of these non-renewals are coming in wildfire-prone areas, and we want to continue to monitor this,” Kane told lawmakers. The record number of non-renewals stood out as one of several indicators Kane outlined that showed a mixed picture of how the private insurance market is or isn’t covering New Mexico homeowners. The state’s top 10 providers suffered major revenue losses in 2024 and 2025 in New Mexico, due to the 2024 South Fork and Salt Fires, she said. But in the decade before that, the carriers largely met their profitability targets in New Mexico. And she noted that no company has pulled out of the state entirely, unlike in California. As for homeowners, premiums have increased at accelerated rates since the pandemic due to supply chain issues for construction materials and recent wildfires. But average insurance premium increases were less than 5% in 2025 and 2026, far less than the 9.3% increases in 2024 and 15% in 2023, Kane noted. Officials with the state’s biggest insurer, State Farm, did not respond to Source NM’s request for comment Wednesday about the rate increases or non-renewals. The company holds more than one-fifth of New Mexico homeowners insurance policies, according to the OSI. Lawmakers at the Tuesday hearing asked Kane about the impact of recent legislative efforts to buttress the Fair Access to Insurance Requirements Plan, often called the “insurer of last resort,” which serves homeowners whose policies are not renewed, along with others who otherwise can’t to secure private market insurance. In 2025, the Legislature gave $10 million to the OSI to help homeowners with FAIR Plan coverage mitigate their homes against wildfire risk, including measures like clearing trees from near structures, installing screens on vents and making roofs more flame resistant. Kane said Tuesday that the grant program is still in its early stages. Still, she said that she is hopeful insurers will see other statewide efforts at mitigating wildfire risk to homes and choose to continue covering homeowners. She also said insurers will soon start offering discounts to homeowners who prove they’ve minimized wildfire risk, she said. “We’ve seen in a number of situations where there were going to be non-renewals. If the homeowner has mitigated … sometimes the non-renewal is canceled,” she said. “And they’re able to keep their insurance.” Source NM is an independent, nonprofit news organization that shines a light on governments, policies and public officials. title: More than 10,000 New Mexico kids have lost federal food assistance in last year, new analysis shows
body: More than 10,000 New Mexico children have lost federal food assistance benefits in the year since Congress enacted a sweeping spending bill, according to a new analysis from a Washington, D.C.-based think tank. The spending bill President Donald Trump signed last July imposed new work requirements and other burdens on households seeking food assistance from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. It also included stiff penalties for states that have high rates of errors in implementing the program, causing states, including New Mexico, to quickly impose new paperwork requirements. The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities’ analysis released Tuesday says those new burdens on states and households have coincided with more than 1.5 million children nationwide losing their SNAP benefits, roughly one-third of the estimated 4.5 million people who lost SNAP since Congress passed the law. The center’s analysis looked at the period between July 2025 and April 2026 and determined that roughly 18,000 New Mexicans lost SNAP in that period, including more than 10,000 children. In a news conference Wednesday morning detailing their analysis, center leaders said the swift drop-off of SNAP recipients should compel Congress to delay penalties for states that don’t reduce errors by deadlines set in the law or to give states more funding to reduce errors. “States are working hard to reduce their error rates, but they’re up against the wall,” Vice President for Food Assistance Ty Jones Cox said. “The law didn’t give them any time or resources to do so, so that creates an enormous incentive for states to slash their error rates by any means necessary, and that’s what we’re seeing: more paperwork, shorter certification periods, more red tape, even if it means eligible families lose benefits they’re entitled to.” New Mexico could face a penalty of at least $150 million if it does not reduce its error rate from 16.8% – which is the third-highest in the nation – to less than 6% by October 2027. The New Mexico Health Care Authority recently imposed new verification requirements for SNAP applicants’ incomes and household sizes, and the authority is working to improve its data collection and caseworker training to minimize the number of SNAP over- and underpayments made to SNAP recipients. The center examined data from 19 states with readily available data regarding children enrolled in SNAP. New Mexico’s proportion of children who lost SNAP – 56% – over the last year was among the highest. Health Care Authority officials did not immediately respond to Source NM’s emailed request for comment Wednesday. More-recent HCA data reviewed by Source NM shows that the trend in SNAP disenrollment has continued through June, with approximately 7,000 additional people losing SNAP between April and June. That HCA data does not specify how many of them are children. The center’s analysts say they cannot identify whether lack of funding or new barriers on households is the primary driver in reducing SNAP enrollment. But they ruled out the possibility that SNAP households’ economic well-being have improved enough in the last year that they no longer need the food assistance. “Grocery prices are still rising,” Jones Cox said. “Unemployment has been largely flat since before the law passed. Real wages have actually declined. People need food assistance today just as much as they did a year ago, and they’re simply being cut off from assistance as states scramble to limit their exposure.” Source NM is an independent, nonprofit news organization that shines a light on governments, policies and public officials. title: Witnesses testify in Farmington man’s double-homicide trial
body: Double-homicide suspect Andrew Whittenberg was reportedly high on methamphetamine, paranoid and asking for help in the early morning hours of Oct. 21, 2024. His drug-fueled state allegedly led to a crime spree that ended in the deaths of Kelly Heath, 45, and Brent Francis, 24, both of Farmington. Whittenberg, 36, is charged with two counts of first-degree murder, aggravated burglary, a second-degree felony; tampering with evidence, a third-degree felony; possession of a firearm by a felon, a third-degree felony; and larceny of a firearm, a fourth-degree felony. Whittenberg’s contact with law enforcement began in the early morning hours, when San Juan County Sheriff’s Deputy Brandon Bull was called at 3:45 a.m. to a home in the Anasazi Estates. Karren Parret reported a man was attempting to get into her home. She identified him in court as Whittenberg, who was shown on a video trying her door handle and asking for help. Despite this being a potential probation violation for Whittenberg, Deputy Bull removed him from the property and drove him to the Animas Valley Mall in Farmington. From there Whittenberg walked down English Road, where Michael Owen said he made eye contact with him through his car’s windshield. “He was crossing the intersection, we made eye contact,” Owen told the jury. “When he crossed in front of the car and the headlights got him, I got a good look.” Owen identified Whittenberg in court as the man he saw around 4:30 a.m. at the intersection of English Road and Largo. What Owen didn’t know was that Whittenberg would reportedly walk to the man’s house in the 4900 block of Kayenta Drive and would allegedly break in by entering through a doggy door at the rear of the home. Linda Owen, who was home, told the jury she came face-to-face with him. “When I opened my bedroom door there was a gentleman standing there. He was yelling, ‘Where’s Kelly at? Where’s Kelly at?’” Linda said, adding Whittenberg then “walked back into the office and started ruffling with things on the desk.” Linda ran into the bedroom, where her daughter-in-law Jessica Curley was hiding with her three children. Curley cried as she testified and listened to her 9-1-1 call that morning. She told dispatch, “There’s a guy with a gun in the house. He’s yelling for someone named Kelly. There’s no one named Kelly here.” Whittenberg left the house, allegedly with an Anderson AR-15 rifle and PSD ammunition that belonged to Michael Owen. It was shortly after 5 a.m. and gunfire started. Isaac Pena, Owen’s neighbor, told the jury he heard three shots. “I was in the military. I knew it was a gunshot,” Pena said, adding he “threw on his body armor” grabbed his own firearm and climbed on his roof to assess the situation. Prosecutor Andrea Reeb asked Pena if he could identify the type of gunfire by sound. Pena said he heard AR-15 gunfire more than a million times, and “the higher pitch ping of the noise sounded exactly like an AR.” Defense Attorney Marie Legrand Miller objected to the testimony saying Pena was not an expert, and 11th Judicial District Court Judge Curtis Gurley sustained her objection. “I’m striking the testimony,” Gurley said and ordered the jury to disregard the statement. Whittenberg reportedly walked to a home in the 2900 block of English Road, where it is alleged he made contact with his former girlfriend Kelly Heath and shot her in the yard. Whittenberg’s brother Anthony Miller was staying in a tent on the property at the time. Anthony told the jury he awoke to the sounds of gunfire and found bullet holes in his vehicle and the dead woman behind it. “I glanced. There was somebody behind my vehicle. It was a lady. Her name was Kelly. She was behind my vehicle. I freaked out. She was bleeding,” Anthony said. “I don’t really know what happened. I wanted to get her medical attention.” Whittenberg’s brother awoke Sham Hawkins by banging on his bedroom window, Hawkins told the jury. Hawkins said Anthony “was very distraught, scared, confused and didn’t want to be in this situation.” Hawkins said Anthony told him, “Andrew was in my yard killing people.” When questioned by Reeb, his brother denied saying that. “I don’t know if I said anything. I heard gunshots. I don’t want to get shot either. I want the police over here. I want to be protected,” Anthony told Reeb. He also repeatedly told Reeb, “I care for him, yes I care for him,” when asked about his relationship with Whittenberg. Legrand Miller also questioned Whittenberg’s brother by asking him if he was being honest. “Yes, I’m honest. If you want to give me a lie-detector test today, I will. I’m honest. I go to church,” Anthony said. “I just seen Kelly behind my vehicle and was concerned about getting her medical attention.” His brother also told Legrand Miller that he is “not afraid” of Whittenberg. Legrand Miller then asked Hawkins if he was a felon and a methamphetamine addict. Hawkins admitted to using methamphetamine to deal with the death of his mother. He also said that he picked up the felony charge in August 2025 and was not a convicted felon at the time of the incident. Hawkins also told Legrand Miller that he used methamphetamine with Whittenberg, whom he had known for nearly 30 years. She asked if Whittenberg acted differently when using the drug. “He definitely acted night and day when he’d do it,” Hawkins said, adding Whittenberg would talk about “the people that loved him trying to do something dirty to him.” Legrand Miller said in her opening statement that Whittenberg was taking methamphetamine on Oct. 21, 2024. Daniel Garcia, who lived along English Road, testified that he came into contact with Whittenberg at 5:15 a.m. “I remember hearing someone at the mailboxes where I live. I heard some guy – a white guy – I went outside and told him, ‘Hey what are you doing,” Garcia said. “He was banging on the sides of the mailboxes. He was spun out. He was tweaked the (expletive) out.” Legrand Miller said in her opening that her client “was in a rough place,” adding he had been wandering around Farmington. Whittenberg reportedly wandered from English Road to Ralph W. Miller, a business in the 3700 block of Herrera Road, where he allegedly met Victor Johnson. Johnson was the first one to arrive at the company that does general distribution and oil field work. He put on the coffee and had some quiet time reading his Bible, when Whittenberg allegedly walked into the business. Johnson recently went blind and was unable to identify Whittenberg in court, but he did pick him out of photo lineup right after the incident. He also identified Whittenberg during a Nov. 8, 2024, preliminary hearing. What Johnson was able to do during the trial was describe Whittenberg’s demeanor the day of the shootings. “He was nervous. He was jumpy. He was breathing hard. He was anxious, very anxious,” Johnson said, adding that Whittenberg asked for a glass of water and a ride to Ramah. “I told him that I had workers coming. Let me get with the workers and we’ll see what we can do,” Johnson said. He asked Whittenberg to go outside and wait on the porch. Whittenberg reportedly complied, but once outside allegedly began shooting. “I heard him yell out an obscenity,” Johnson said. Reeb told him to go ahead and say it. “He yelled out, ‘You mother (expletive) and then I heard bang, bang, bang, bang. He was shooting into Brent’s truck. It was close-range, 30-40 foot away.” Brent Francis, the second victim, had arrived at work moments before and backed into a parking place at Ralph W. Miller. Johnson said he looked out the front window. “I could see him shooting into the driver’s side of the vehicle,” Johnson said, adding he left out the backdoor. Francis was shot multiple times and died at the scene. A ballistic expert, Matthew Bustmante, testified that the bullet casings found at the scene came from the Anderson rifle stolen from the Owen’s residence. That same rifle was found by Farmington Police, discarded in a nearby alley behind Theodore Martinez’s house. Martinez testified that he saw Whittenberg “come out of the alley.” He identified Whittenberg in court and said he was 85% sure it was the same man. Whittenberg also was allegedly captured at 5:48 a.m. on a video recording from a home on Best Street. title: Law enforcement identifies man suspected of hitting bicyclist south of Durango
body: An Aztec man suspected of hitting a bicyclist Tuesday south of Durango admitted to drinking three beers prior to the crash and had an open bottle of Southern Comfort in the truck, according to an arrest affidavit. Thomas Huntsman, 39, was arrested on suspicion of felony vehicular assault, drunken driving, driving with an open container of alcohol and driving without insurance. He had been released from the La Plata County Jail as of Wednesday. The crash was reported shortly after 6:30 p.m. near County Road 302 and U.S. Highway 550, about 3 miles south of Durango. Bystanders at the scene told authorities the passenger-side mirror hit multiple riders, but only one went down and under the pickup truck and trailer. According to the Colorado State Patrol, Huntsman drifted into a turn lane, hit a cyclist, ran over a stop sign and struck a deer fence. The cycling community identified the injured cyclist as Elliott Saslow, 32, who coaches with Durango Devo, a local cycling group. Saslow suffered broken bones, including a broken pelvis, according to those in the cycling community. He was taken to Mercy Hospital in serious condition. Huntsman refused to participate in a voluntary field sobriety test at the scene of the crash, and a search warrant was granted for an blood-alcohol test, according to the affidavit. While at Mercy Hospital, Huntsman allegedly told law enforcement he was drinking out of a Southern Comfort bottle in the pickup truck. State troopers were unable to locate proof of insurance for Huntsman’s pickup truck. Huntsman was allegedly agitated and aggressive at the scene of the crash. He made statements saying he does not care about cyclists and was vulgar toward cyclists at the scene, according to the affidavit. Todd Wells, a Durango cyclist and former Olympian, arrived at the scene about 10 minutes after the crash. He said Huntsman tried to approach Saslow as he lay on the ground surrounded by other cyclists who were trying to render aid. The driver was acting “belligerent” toward Saslow, Wells said. “The guy who was clearly drunk was trying to get to Elliott and we were trying to keep that person away from Elliott,” he said. Police arrived before any physical altercations could occur between Huntsman and the cyclists, Wells said. Deputies also reported Huntsman standing over the downed cyclist acting aggressive, according to the affidavit. Wells said the typical route for cyclists in that area takes them down Highway 550 for two minutes, as they move from one county road to the next. The turning lane where Saslow was hit is the wider part of the road where drivers have more room to pass. “It’s where you finally feel somewhat safe – where you’re in the shoulder, you’re out of the motorists’ way, there’s plenty of room for passing,” Wells said. title: One killed, two seriously injured in car crash last weekend north of Durango
body: A Durango woman was killed in a three-car crash Saturday on U.S. Highway 550 just north of Durango. Sandra “Sandy” Elliott, 79, was flown to Penrose Hospital in Colorado Springs before dying from her injuries, said La Plata County Coroner Jann Smith. The crash was reported about 4:45 a.m. near mile marker 26, according to the Colorado State Patrol. Elliott was traveling north in a Ford Flex when the southbound driver of a Nissan Murano swerved across the center line and hit Elliott head-on, said State Trooper Sherri Mendez. “The front left of the Ford Flex was struck by the front left of Nissan Murano,” she said. The impact sent the Ford Flex rotating and careening off the right side of the road, landing in the northbound ditch. The Nissan then struck a Toyota Tacoma traveling behind Elliott, pushing it backward from the point of impact. The Nissan then rolled and landed in the southbound lane, Mendez said. The cause of the crash, and whether drugs or alcohol were involved, remained under investigation as of Wednesday. Mendez declined to provide the names of the other parties involved, citing the ongoing investigation. Elliott’s daughter, Allisa Oliger, said Elliott’s partner of five years, Thomas “Steve” Bettis, 76, was a passenger in the vehicle. He suffered critical injuries and was fighting for his life as of Wednesday, she said. Bettis was taken to Penrose in serious condition, she said. The driver of the Nissan, an 18-year-old man, was taken to an unknown hospital with serious injuries. The driver of the Toyota Tacoma, a 26-year-old man, reported no injuries, Mendez said. Elliott is survived by three children and four grandchildren. Her daughter described her as strong-minded, intelligent, brave and truthful. “This was completely unexpected,” Oliger said. “She was healthy, active, still working with some private clients.” She described her mother as being “at the top of her game.” Elliott, originally from Portland, Oregon, moved to Durango in 1974. She worked as a CPA, starting at Frederick Zink & Elliott, PC, and eventually started her own firm called Elliott Meadows & Associates, LLC. Although she took some private clients, she officially retired around 2015-2017. She was an avid quilter, traveler and golfer. “She lived for golfing,” Oliger said. She was actively involved with Dalton Ranch and previously involved with the League of Women Voters and the Durango Chamber of Commerce. Oliger said both Elliott and Bettis received excellent care from hospital staff as well as from first responders at the scene. jrooney@durangoherald.com  Choose from several print and digital subscription packages Sign up for our daily email newsletter or to receive breaking news delivered to your inbox: © 2026 Tri-City Record |         Ballantine Communications, Inc. title: Republican challenger narrowly outraises N.M. U.S. Rep. Vasquez, but trails with cash on hand
body: New campaign finance reports show that the campaign for an Albuquerque Republican challenging incumbent U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.) in the Nov. 3 general election has narrowly raised more money than his opponent, although Vasquez’s campaign has a strong cash-on-hand advantage. The latest campaign finance filings, which cover April through June, offer a glimpse into a competitive race for a district that represents much of southern New Mexico and a portion of Albuquerque. Vasquez first won election to the 2nd Congressional District seat, which was previously held by Republican Yvette Herrell, in 2022 by less than one percentage point. Greg Cunningham, the Republican nominee who handily won his party’s primary for the race after his opponent bowed out, announced that he raised nearly $902,000 in the second quarter of this year – just shy of $1,000 more than Vasquez. Vasquez’s campaign has about three times the amount of cash on hand, though. “There are some individuals and organizations who feel that CD 2 will be a competitive race. Usually, people don’t like to contribute money unless they feel like the candidate has a shot,” Brian Sanderoff, president of the Albuquerque-based firm Research and Polling Inc., told Source NM. Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham signed off on redrawn congressional districts in late 2021, following the 2020 U.S. Census. That redistricting introduced portions of Albuquerque, which Sanderoff said are considered Democratic strongholds, into the otherwise rural district. “Greg Cunningham does have one challenge to address in whether the mood of the nation could impact his competitiveness … most analysts feel the Democrats will flip the U.S. House,” Sanderoff said. “His strategy is going to have to be to cut his losses in Bernalillo County.” Cunningham in a statement announcing his fundraising efforts said he believes the latest fundraising reports show that district residents want “a Congressman who actually shows up for them, not a far-left radical like Gabe Vasquez who voted to raise taxes on families and against securing our border.” “New Mexico deserves better, and this quarter proves our district is ready to flip,” he wrote. Vasquez’s campaign manager, Patricia Socarras Santiago, in a statement to Source NM, wrote that Cunningham has shown an allegiance to President Donald Trump and raised hundreds of thousands of dollars in “MAGA money.” “New Mexicans cannot be bought off and they deserve someone who is actually fighting for them,” she wrote. “That fighter has always been Gabe Vasquez, and that’s why New Mexicans will re-elect him in November.” Source NM is an independent, nonprofit news organization that shines a light on governments, policies and public officials. title: Abundance of talent on display as Connie Mack World Series begins play this weekend
body: FARMINGTON – The rosters are set and the final planning phases are being made as Friday’s opening day of the pool play portion of the Connie Mack World Series rapidly approaches. Here’s a look at some of the top players coming into the series from across the country that we’ll be keeping an eye on as the series plays out. Browning took part in last year’s CMWS as a member of PPA White Sox Scout Team. A recent commit University of Arkansas, Browning has been one of the top producers for the Pleasant Grove (Texas) Hawks, hitting .363 with seven home runs and 36 runs batted in during his junior season. He was selected to the THSBCA 4A All-State Team as a 1st Team SS and to the TSWA 4A All-State Team as a 3rd Team SS. Sullivan, who pitched for the Redskins in last year’s CMWS, stands at 6-foot, 188 pounds and has a fastball consistently in the mid-90s that has reached as high as 97 miles per hour. As a senior at Walsh Jesuit (Ohio) High, Sullivan went 3-1 with a 0.90 ERA and 89 strikeouts in 46.2 innings. His career ERA was 1.30 ERA over 145 innings with 256 strikeouts. The Warriors finished the season as Division II state runners-up. Sullivan plans to play college ball next season at the University of Tennessee. Another returning starter from last year, Viars has grown on and off the field to become one of the most important players on this summer’s roster. “He has really grown up even beyond what he was last year,” said D-Bat head coach Ryan Bonesio. “He had a hit peak around .400, and he was one of the state leaders in home runs. That's to go with the fact that his impact defensively is unmatched.” Viars, a recent commit to West Virginia, has the potential to be something special as a catcher. “I know that he's got an opportunity to work into eventually becoming a catcher at West Virginia, as well,” Bonesio said. “He's a fantastic player and he's going to be a big part of how we do in this tournament.” The recent Baylor commit comes off an impressive season at Montgomery (Texas) High School, in which he recorded a .387 batting average with six home runs, 25 runs batted in and 17 stolen bases. A star infielder at Boswell High School in Fort Worth, Thacker has also excelled at powerlifting, recently winning the Texas Class 6A state title in the 181-lb. weight class, lifting a career-best total of 1,630 pounds. Thacker has played a dozen games for the D-Bat United this summer, recording a .273 batting average with 10 runs batter in and 11 runs scored. “Thacker is a defender and a good bat,” said Bonesio. “He's a pretty good pitcher too, so we like to use him in the middle to bottom third of the lineup.” Thacker has also been proficient on the mound as a relief pitcher for D-Bat United, striking out seven and allowing just four hits over five innings of work. He is currently committed to playing baseball at Navarro College in Corsicana. An incoming senior at Anderson (Texas) High School and commit to the University of Texas, Rippy has been a member of the team from the beginning of the summer. Rippy is coming off a strong high school season, in which he earned Most Valuable Player honors and Offensive Player of the Year. Blue Valley (Kansas) High’s Ethan Carswell is a switch-hitting middle infielder who recently announced his intent to play collegiate ball at the University of Southern California. Carswell batted .308 for the Redbirds this summer. A recent commit to the University of Texas after having recently graduate from Waxahachie (Texas) High, Robinson finished third among Class 6A baseball players with 11 home runs this past season. He finished the season with 61 runs batted in and only seven strikeouts. title: Fanfare and excitement build as Connie Mack World Series opens Friday at Ricketts Park
body: FARMINGTON – The game can change in the blink of an eye. One minute, your favorite team is up four runs and three outs away from securing a victory. Before you know it, a base hit follows a walk and a hit batter, and suddenly you can feel the drama build. From the perspective of a player or manager, the swings and shifts in momentum can be physically taxing. For the fan — trust me — it’s a whole different experience. As a passionate lover of baseball, I’m also the first to admit that the world is coming to an end when my favorite team loses what might well be a meaningless game in the first week of May. I’m also the guy who will break down why a supposedly meaningless win by that same team the very next day is precisely why it will win the division, the league and, eventually, the World Series. That’s the seesaw lifestyle of baseball fans. The stars have to align a certain way. The decisions made in clubhouses and owners boxes that are completely out of our control are the very reason we pore over box scores and transactions. Supporters of high school, collegiate or travel teams go through many of the same emotional conflicts. Tack on the costs of being a booster or a coach responsible for keeping the team fed and transported from one place to another, and suddenly the passion for the sport becomes deeply personal and quite expensive. These are important things to remember when you’re sitting in the stands and chiding the decisions made by a coach or a manager. Not only is he keeping his eye on the action occurring on the field, but he is also responsible for making sure his team will be ready to play later tonight or tomorrow. Or, as will be the case for a majority of teams this week, he is balancing the plans that have to be made for that uncomfortable trip home. The Connie Mack World Series will be one of a few massive moments in the careers of rising baseball talents. For some, it may be their final moment on the field. For a few others, it may be just the beginning. In addition to the historic names of Ken Griffey, Jr., Barry Larkin and Edgar Martinez, who graced the field at Ricketts Patrk before combining to hit more than 1,100 home runs in their respective careers in Major League Baseball, there’s names you may not be as familiar with who’ve also had a significant impact on their MLB rosters. Yan Gomes was an MLB All-Star catcher and World Series champion with the 2019 Washington Nationals who will be enshrined in the Connie Mack World Series Hall of Fame this week. Gomes competed in the Connie Mack World Series with the Florida Bombers of Miami. Born in Mogi das Cruzes, Gomes went on to build an outstanding Major League career with the Toronto Blue Jays, Cleveland Guardians, Washington, Oakland Athletics, and Chicago Cubs. And if you’re looking for current stars linked to the CMWS, look no further than New York Mets starting right fielder Carson Benge, who was one of the stars for the 2023 Enid (Oklahoma) Majors. Either way, it’s up to you to respect the moment and the sport. If that’s your favorite team rushing out to celebrate the championship, cheer loud and proud. If that’s not your team showering the winning coach with a Gatorade bath following the conclusion of the CMWS, that’s alright, too. We’ve all been on both sides of that celebratory moment, and that’s precisely why we love baseball. Because it’s just a matter of days before we do it all over again. Enjoy the tournament. title: Pair of Farmington High grads sign to extend athletic careers
body: FARMINGTON – A pair of multi-sport athletes recently graduated from Farmington High School recently announced their intention to extend their academic and athletic careers by signing on with colleges. Danny Hagstrom, who doubled as a pitcher and outfielder this past season for the Scorpions, signed his letter of intent to join the baseball roster at Lassen Community College in Susanville, California. Hagstrom, who achieved success both in baseball and football at Farmington High, joins a Cougars baseball team coming off a 28-15 season and advancing to the California Community College Athletic Association postseason. Hagstrom was a solid contributor on the field. Among his season highlights at the plate last season was a 3-RBI performance including a home run in a district clash at Rio Rancho last April, followed by a 4-for-5 game against Cleveland High. The Cougars, coached by Frank Avilla, have been a powerhouse in junior college baseball in recent years. Under Avilla’s leadership, the Cougars recorded their most wins in over 20 years in 2022, 2024 through 2026, and tallied over 120 program wins across the past five seasons. The Cougars have now made five consecutive NORCAL Regional appearances (2022–2026), and in both 2024 and 2025, Lassen had the honor of hosting back-to-back NORCAL Regionals—the first time that’s happened since 2004. Avilla is entering his 17th season with Lassen College baseball and his 16th as head coach. His teams have averaged 20-plus wins per season since 2017. Hagstrom was also a key contributor on the FHS football team, recording nearly 100 tackles in three seasons on the Scorpions football team. Also signing his letter of intent was recent Farmington High graduate Santiago Gonzales, who has agreed to attend Allan Hancock College in Santa Maria, California. Gonzales played a variety of sports during his 4-year stint at FHS, including football, track and field, baseball and wrestling. On the gridiron, Gonzales doubled as a linebacker and running back, recording nearly 200 tackles in three seasons as a Scorpion. The Bulldogs, coming off a 4-6 campaign last season, are a part of the Western State Conference and are led by head coach Rick Aguilar. title: Muddy mess in downtown Aztec reminiscent of 2014
body: An intense lighting storm and heavy rain that began with high winds struck Aztec and surrounding areas on Monday evening, turning the skies a yellowish-orange. The result was downed trees, debris, damaged roofs and fences, and a muddy mess on Main Avenue and at the Aztec Museum and Pioneer Village. More heavy rain was predicted for Tuesday evening, a repeat of what Aztec experienced in 2014. One Aztec resident shared her frightening, stormy experience. One moment, Kathleen Holmes was feeding her horses under a sunny sky. Minutes later, she retreated inside her Knickerbocker Hill home along Road 173 as a violent, fast-moving storm approached. By the time she reached her upstairs window, the wind was shaking the house so hard an elk antler crashed from the fireplace onto the floor. Outside, a 100-pound metal arbor was tossed into a tree. San Juan County Public Relations Manager Devin Neeley said areas including Aztec, Road 3000 and Flora Vista saw the worst of the sudden storm. While Farmington was largely spared, the county received multiple reports of downed power lines and tree limbs blocking public roads. Holmes, who has lived in the area for 35 years, said the storm approached rapidly from the east around 6 p.m., with lightning strikes growing closer until her house felt like it was “sitting kind of at a bull’s-eye” “We have windows facing the east, and I was upstairs looking at some big picture – through some big picture windows – and I saw the storm coming, and suddenly trees were landing on my roof, and on the roof of the porch right below me,” Holmes said. According to Holmes an aspen and a cottonwood tree were pulled up by the roots, and sheet metal from a hay barn flew five acres away. The heavy metal arbor, which Holmes made herself as a blacksmith artist, was ripped from the ground. “I saw the wind pick it up and just shoot it off,” she said. “I saw it just traveling through the air, and it’s all wrapped and bent around a tree like a piece of wire.” While emergency services reported winds around 25 to 30 mph, Holmes believes they were much stronger, comparing it to her past experience surviving a tornado in Virginia. “This was a lot closer to 70 mph,” she said. “I just don't see how a 35 mph can do that kind of damage.” Though there is a massive cleanup ahead for her property, Holmes remained positive. “You know, it could have been a lot worse, and the horses are OK, and we’re OK, so that’s all that really matters in the long run, right?” Holmes said. Aztec Police Chief and Co-Interim City Manager Troy Morris described the mud damage caused by the storm Monday night in Aztec as overwhelming. “It came all the way down from Blanco, got the museum, and you can see where it even passed the museum, all into the parking lots here and everywhere,” he said. Morris said electricity was off on the south side of town and crews were out cleaning up the mud both Monday night and Tuesday morning, beginning at 8 a.m. Describing some of the damage, Morris said the First Baptist Church had part of its roof blown off, the fence across the street at Park Avenue School was knocked down, the fence at Hartman Park was damaged, High Country Chevrolet suffered mud damage as did the Aztec Museum, the Splash Pad near City Hall and Pioneer Village. Co-Interim City Manager Ed Kotyk said the splash park would be closed indefinitely. Angela Watkins, Aztec Library director, said the power went out for awhile and she woke up this morning to something that looked like “Louisiana’s hurricane … broken tree branches, the debris all over the roads.” Kotyk said the power was out for about an hour in a part of Aztec and was still out at 10:30 p.m. on the south side. He confirmed that a lightning strike took out a transformer. Morris said city employees were being assisted by a private company because another storm was expected on Tuesday afternoon or evening. Clearing the drains under Main Avenue was their priority, he said. The mud damage was worse than in 2014, Kotyk said. Former Aztec City Commissioner and Museum board treasurer Jack Scott described the event as a “continuing saga,” because the drains have needed cleaning for years. In 2014, the city spent $50,000 to clean up mud and debris from heavy rains on consecutive days, he said. Aztec Museum Executive Director Joan Monninger said there was “a little bit” of water damage in the front upstairs entryway, but it’s fixable. “The Pioneer Village grounds are a mess,” she said, adding that “fortunately, no water or mud got into the storage areas or the lower level of the main museum building. She said Scott was a “real hero with all of this beginning last night when he got me out of the building once the mud had subsided.” Monninger said there will be plenty of work to do in the coming days. title: NTU radio station KCZY outfits new system to increase reliability
body: NTU radio station KCZY outfits new system to increase reliability  Tuesday, 11 February 2025 13:53 gallupsun CROWNPOINT — Navajo Technical University radio station KCZY 107.3 FM received an upgrade to its transmission system to ensure its continuous 6000W broadcast covering a majority of the Eastern Navajo Nation Jan. 28. Broadcast engineer Jim Burt and NTU-IT Specialists Dody Begay and Chris Yazzie switched KCZY’s terrestrial transmission from the original system to a new direct STL system. The installation increases reliability during electrical outages, reduces the recovery time from brownouts, and mitigates other failures that cause the station to go off-air."The new equipment also upgraded the sound quality on our tuner radio for a more enjoyable user experience. title: Scheduled water outage for Feb. 10
body: Scheduled water outage for Feb. 10 Sunday, 09 February 2025 11:42 gallupsun Dallago Corporation has been contracted by the City of Gallup to install a new waterline along Rico Street from Highway 66 south toward the new fire station at the corner of Rico Street and Bengal Road. The City of Gallup Water Department will need to shut down water service temporarily while the contractor installs a new 8-inch water valve. The affected area will be from the intersection of Highway 66 and Rico Street to the south ending at Bengal Road. The water shut off will take place Feb. 10 from 4 pm to 8 pm.  Surrounding areas may experience low water pressure. For any questions, call Utility Dispatch at (505) 863-1200 or after hours dispatch at 833-863-1212.

title: Overdose deaths decline in New Mexico
body: Overdose deaths decline in New Mexico Tuesday, 07 January 2025 14:35 gallupsun SANTA FE — New Mexico mortality data show a decrease in drug overdose deaths statewide for the second consecutive year since 2021.Overdose deaths have declined 8% statewide since 2021 when the number of overdose deaths peaked at 1,029 deaths, according to data compiled by the epidemiology team at the New Mexico Department of Health. In 2022, New Mexico had 997 overdose deaths. That number has fallen to 948 overdose deaths in 2023.“These decreases are welcome news, but there is still much more to do to reduce the problem of substance misuse in New Mexico,” NMDOH Interim Secretary Gina DeBlassie said. “Substance misuse is a multifaceted and complex public health issue, and we...

title: Navajo Nation Council mourns the passing of Diné College President Dr. Charles M. Roessel
body: Navajo Nation Council mourns the passing of Diné College President Dr. Charles M. Roessel Monday, 06 January 2025 14:53 gallupsun WINDOW ROCK, Ariz. — The 25th Navajo Nation Council is deeply saddened by the passing of Diné College President Dr. Charles M. Roessel, who passed away in the early morning of Jan. 6, as confirmed by official notice from Diné College.“Dr. Roessel was a tireless advocate for tribal education and a visionary leader whose work transformed Diné College from a two-year institution to a four-year university,” Speaker Crystalyne Curley said. “His leadership and dedication were pivotal in shaping educational opportunities for Navajo students, and his efforts have left an indelible mark on the future of our people.”Before taking on the role of Diné College President, Roessel...
